GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Chances for light precipitation (valley rain, mountain snow above 10,000 feet) continue through the weekend as a low pressure system, currently spinning off the California coast, traverses the Intermountain West.
GJT.text:
HAZARDOUS WEATHER POSSIBLE THROUGH FRIDAY:

Remnant tropical moisture will once again take aim at the Intermountain West and Rockies. The first wave of this deeper moisture arrives to the Four Corners region by sunrise and track northeastward across the remainder of eastern Utah and western Colorado through the day before being swept away on Friday. A full array of hazards are possible with this prolonged event including river flooding, flash flooding, strong to severe thunderstorms, and snow above 12,000-13,000 feet. A Flood watch has been issued for parts of southeast Utah and southwest Colorado beginning 12 PM tomorrow and persisting through 12 PM Friday.

The 21/00Z KGJT RAOB is sitting at 2/3 of an inch of PWAT which is already anomalous and in the 90th percentile. Impressive for mid October but just the tip of the iceberg. GOES All Layer PWAT imagery is showing the nose of true tropical mositure moving into south-central AZ this evening and should arrive to the 4 Corners in the pre-sunrise hours. PWAT is projected to push above an inch by sunset at GJT which would be a new daily record and some 300+ percent of normal. So the stage will once again be set for excessive rainfall rates and impressive total precipitation amounts through the event. This moisture will also effectively lighten and destabilize the atmosphere and allow even minimal lift to produce ascent and efficiently squeeze out this anomalous PWAT. Ascent over the next few days will aided by a strong SubTrop jet aloft tomorrow followed by the Polar jet on Thursday which is associated with the main upstream trough over the West. CAPE will be modest at best over the 4 Corners region the next few afternoons. The wind profile will however be impressive...with low level east/southeast flow over-topped by the strong southwest flow aloft. BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Beyond this weekend, most guidance does (at least briefly) suggest that temperatures will warm back into the 60s across the plains, with generally dry conditions.
BOU.text:
The next couple of days will be dominated by broad south- southwesterly flow aloft, as a strong trough to the west slowly drifts off to the northeast, while a ridge slowly builds just to the east of our forecast area. Embedded in the flow is some extremely impressive moisture. Forecast PW and 500/700mb specific humidity increases significantly over the next 24 hours or so, with most of these values reaching standardized anomalies of 4-6 sigma... well outside climatology for this time of year. Of course, the flow aloft is rather unfavorable for significant orographic precipitation here. We should still manage scattered rain and snow showers both Wednesday and Thursday, but the more impressive rainfall totals will be confined to southwest Colorado. The pattern will also favor above normal temperatures across the region, with snow levels sitting around 12-14kft, and highs in the 70s across most of the plains.

The mid-level flow strengthens a bit on Friday as a shortwave rotates around the parent trough axis from southeastern Utah into western Wyoming. 700-500mb flow approaches 30-40kt Friday afternoon with a generally dry/subsident airmass... which should allow for a few gusts of 30-40 mph across the eastern plains. A fairly strong lee cyclone over northern Colorado would likely limit wind gusts along and north of I-76, meaning that the northwest Denver metro could see a fairly calm day while the southeast metro ends up rather breezy. These details are hard to pinpoint but should become more clear over the next couple days where CAMs will be available. Across the mountains, there could be a few showers during the day but most of the moisture exits the area pretty quickly.

While the main trough ejects out of the region on Friday, guidance is insistent that at least one piece of this trough will be left over the desert southwest. PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Saturday through Tuesday...While one low center lingers across the Four Corners, the northern piece cross the northern Rockies and pushes a cold front south into eastern CO Saturday morning.
PUB.text:
Thursday...All indications point to Thursday as seeing the greatest impacts from this Pacific storm. As the low continues moving east across CA and NV through the day, an upper shortwave rotates across AZ and into the Four Corners region. This upper support, coupled with increasing proximity of the system, will mean periods of heavy rainfall across western CO and along the Continental Divide through the entire day. The focus area continues to be the southwest mts, with total additional rainfall amounts ranging from an inch up to 2.75 inches possible through the day, while the remainder of the higher terrain could see around half an inch. SPC shows the Marginal area for strong to severe thunderstorms creeping into the southwestern corner of the state, giving a nod to the abundant moisture plus upper level support, so periods of heavy convective rainfall falling on already saturated ground and some high elevation snow pack leading to excessive runoff will be possible, hence the ongoing flood Watch. Those living or traveling across the southwest mountains should stay weather aware through the rest of the week, and have multiple ways to receive weather warnings. As for the eastern plains, dry and continued warm conditions anticipated, though the upper ridge axis finally pushes east out of the area. Look for highs in the 60s for the high valleys, and 70s to lower 80s for the plains.

Friday...Friday will be an interesting day as the system starts to weaken and split into two pieces by the evening. The northern piece pushes up into MT, while the southern piece drops south and tries to gather some strength over the Desert SW. Rain totals of an additional .40 of an inch for the eastern San Juans, and up to a tenth of an inch elsewhere, are forecast, then showers and isolated thunderstorms push along the southern border and up across the far southeast corner through the late afternoon and evening. CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Long range models start to disagree at the beginning of the work week, with the GFS suggesting a strong upper-level low diving southward out of Canada into the northwestern CONUS.
CYS.text: Active weather continues for Friday as the upper-level low across northern Nevada continues to push eastwards towards western Wyoming. A fairly strong, southerly, upper-level jet starts to move overhead Friday morning as the upper-level low pushes into Utah. With much of the region downstream of the upper-level trough axis and portions of the CWA within the left exit region of the jet, synoptic forcing will increase significantly from previous days. The trough starts to elongate overnight Friday, per the GFS and ECMWF, with the upper- level jet strengthening to around 100kts by Saturday morning. Unfortunately, very strong 500mb cyclonic vorticity advection (CVA) will develop across Montana, favoring the deepening of the northern portion of the system. This will lead to split flow developing across the Intermountain west, with the northern branch remaining much stronger than the southern branch. The southern branch looks to be the primary forcing mechanism for precipitation, so as this start to weaken, precipitation will decrease across the region. Similarly, the 700mb low will develop Friday morning before pushing northeastward and starting to elongate with the upper-level system. This will, once again, push the best forcing off the north with more modest forcing expected across the CWA and very weak 700mb flow developing for Saturday morning. Despite the less favorable evolution of this system, precipitation chances are expected to increase from southwest to northeast across the CWA Friday morning through Friday evening. Precipitation will remain mostly rain as 700mb temperatures stay fairly warm in the 5 to 8C range Friday evening. A strong cold front will accompany this system and will drop 700mb temperatures into the 0 to 4C range by early Saturday morning. With cooling temperatures at 700mb, rain across the Sierra Madre and Snowy ranges should change over to mostly snow overnight Friday into Saturday morning. SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: The trailing wave swinging around Arizona now looks to redevelop into a closed low which will then linger over the area. As such, there is now increasing likelihood for cool and unsettled weather to remain in place through the weekend.
SLC.text:
The large-scale pattern this evening consists of a closed low spinning off the central California coast while Utah remains under a southerly flow ahead of it. An upper jet rounding the base of the low and punching through Arizona this evening is helping to spread tropical moisture northward. Across Utah, PWATs currently range from 0.6-0.9 inches, which is already close to the 99th percentile of climatology. Increased moisture advection will only push these values higher over the next couple of days.

As the jet arrives over Utah, increasing upper diffluence may lead to some isolated shower activity tonight, mainly over northwest Utah. As the deeper moisture arrives after 10z, expect precipitation activity to start increasing across southern Utah. This precipitation will become more widespread across southern and central Utah through the day Wednesday. Models indicate a brief decrease in precipitation Wednesday night before increasing again areawide for Thursday. Areas of moderate to heavy precipitation is expected Wednesday and Thursday, and will be aided in part by potentially strong to severe convection as suggested by hi-res models. If instability does not become inhibited too much by cloud cover, there will be plenty of shear (40-55+ kt of 0-6km shear) and low-level helicity to work with across southern Utah on Wednesday and across a significant portion of the forecast area on Thursday for a few of the stronger storms to produce strong winds, hail, and even an outside chance of a tornado. There is currently a Marginal Risk for Severe Storms across southern Utah on Wednesday and across southern through weest-central Utah on Thursday. Additionally, with the heavy rain, there is also a Slight Risk of Excessive Rainfall across southern Utah on Wednesday and across southern through east-central Utah on Thursday. BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Drying conditions and near normal temperatures will return for the weekend thanks to a building ridge of high pressure over the West Coast.
BOI.text: Drying conditions and near normal temperatures will return for the weekend thanks to a building ridge of high pressure over the West Coast. By late Sunday, long range forecast models have once again converged on a closed low pressure system moving onshore and slowly east over the area through the early part of next week. This pattern would bring cooler and wetter conditions yet again by early next week. The highest chances for precipitation would be over the west-central Idaho mountains. With how highly variable and volatile the synoptic pattern has been even just within 24 hours of this forecast, forecaster confidence is low at this time.
